title: FR-D3 T1 CRITICAL — a freshness verdict must not be refreshed by a write that did not read the file
description:
THE FR-D3 HEADLINE, and it outranks task #35. PROVEN by executable check; full reasoning in docs/foundations/03-storage.md sections 2, 3 F1 and 4 T1.

MECHANISM. Staleness confidence is computed from file_mtime versus the file on disk (src/tools/intelligence.ts:296-303, and withStaleness at dispatcher-memory.ts:63). That design is sound. The defect is that set_file_notes re-stats the file UNCONDITIONALLY on every write — dispatcher-memory.ts:367 const file_mtime = getFileMtime(fp, projectRoot) and :368 for content_hash — regardless of which fields the agent actually supplied. Meanwhile FileNotesRepo.upsert wraps every content column in COALESCE(?, col), so omitted fields are preserved. The two combine: a write that supplies one field refreshes the freshness evidence for ALL fields, including the ones it did not touch and did not read.

PROVEN, harness output quoted in the domain doc section 2. Agent A writes a full note, confidence high. The file is then rewritten and is 72 hours newer, confidence correctly reports stale with 72h drift — the feature works. Agent B then writes ONLY purpose and never opens the file. Confidence flips back to high while A's executive_summary, which now describes code that no longer exists, is served unchanged.

WHY THIS IS THE WORST DEFECT IN THE DOMAIN. Agent rule AR-02 is CRITICAL priority and says: call get_file_notes before opening any file, open only if notes are absent or stale. So the forged freshness signal does not merely misinform, it instructs the next agent NOT to read the real file. Under charter section 10.3's scale the unsearchable-index defect scores IRRELEVANT — zero results is loud enough to redirect a reader — while this scores MISLEADING, the bucket the charter singles out as the one that matters and nobody measures.

PRIOR ART that drove the ranking. STALE, arXiv:2605.06527, defines this exact shape as implicit conflict: a new observation invalidates an earlier memory without syntactic negation, with no later utterance marking the obsolescence. Their Type II propagated case is this defect precisely — file_mtime changes and thereby invalidates executive_summary, which nothing updates. Headline number and the reason this cannot be left to downstream readers: the best evaluated model reaches 55.2% accuracy at recognising its own invalid memories and existing memory frameworks score below 10%.

TARGET. Refresh file_mtime and content_hash only when the write supplies the content those fields certify. A partial write leaves the verdict alone and the row keeps saying stale until someone re-reads.

REJECTED, with reasons, see doc section 4 T1: make the agent pass file_mtime explicitly — moves a correctness guarantee onto caller discipline, which this project has eight-plus occurrences of evidence against. Drop the freshness feature — the feature is right and the STALE result argues it should exist. Per-field timestamps — correct but a schema change across the widest table plus every read path; revisit only if FR-D2 wants per-field provenance anyway.

BINDING. tests/storage/retrieval-integrity.test.ts, describe block "Freshness cannot be laundered by a write that did not read the file". The assertion is PINNED as a defect: it currently asserts high and must become stale in the same commit that fixes this.

KILL SWITCH. If the fix makes stale the common verdict in practice, the feature is net-negative and should be removed rather than tuned — a signal that always says stale is a slower way of saying "always open the file". Measure before tuning.</parameter>
</invoke>

title: FR-D3 T3 — FileNotesRepo.upsert uses two different null coercions in one method, so whether a field can be cleared depends on which field it is
description:
PROVEN. src/repositories/file-notes.repo.ts. Lines 42-45 build mtime, branch, hash and exec_summary with `?? null`; lines 65-67 pass purpose, notes, layer and complexity as `data.X || null`. Combined with COALESCE(?, col) in the UPDATE clause this produces two opposite behaviours in one method.

MEASURED across seven fields, each set to "SET" then rewritten with an empty string. CLEARED (the ?? group): executive_summary, git_branch, content_hash. IGNORED (the || group): purpose, notes, layer, complexity — the empty string collapses to NULL, COALESCE keeps the old value, and the field can never be cleared by any caller. Same method, same call shape, opposite result, nothing documents it.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS. purpose and notes are exactly the fields a later agent would want to correct after finding an earlier note wrong, and they are the ones that cannot be corrected. This compounds task #64: the stale content that gets re-certified as fresh is also the content that cannot be cleared. Engram is already append-only in practice by accident — handoff #5 records that there is no update_convention, no delete_convention, and decisions cannot be edited.

TARGET. `??` throughout, one rule: an explicit null clears, an omitted key preserves, "" is stored as "". State the rule in the tool description.

REJECTED. `||` throughout — consistent, and makes every field permanently uncorrectable, which would ratify the accident as design. Leave it and document the split — documentation is not a binding per charter section 7, and it does not survive the next field being added by copy-paste.

BINDING. tests/storage/retrieval-integrity.test.ts, describe "Field coercion is uniform". Pinned: it currently asserts the split and must collapse to a single expectation when this lands.

Related: task #60 (D4's chimera framing) and task #64.</parameter>
</invoke>

title: FR-D3 T5 — delete deleted_at: four tables carry a soft-delete column that nothing reads and nothing writes
description:
PROVEN by grep over the whole src/ tree. src/migrations.ts:593-600 adds deleted_at to decisions, file_notes, tasks and sessions. Those five lines are the ONLY occurrences of the identifier in the entire source tree. Zero readers, zero writers. No repository filters on it, no route filters on it, no dispatcher sets it.

This is the sixth instance of this project's recurring pattern — a capability that exists where the live path cannot reach it — and the purest, because here there is not even an unreachable implementation. There is only the column.

WHY NOT HARMLESS. It is a loaded gun for the next author, who will reasonably assume the read paths honour it. Proven in the binding test: soft-delete a file note by setting deleted_at, and FileNotesRepo.getAll() still returns it. Anyone building a delete feature on this column would ship something that reports success and deletes nothing.

TARGET. Delete the four columns.

REJECTED. Implement soft delete — no feature asks for it; building a delete semantic nobody requested across four tables and every read path, on the strength of four ALTER TABLEs, is how the dead surface got here in the first place. If deletion is wanted it should be designed, not inferred from a column. Leave it as harmless — see above, it is not.

NOTE FOR WHOEVER DOES THIS. Dropping columns is a schema migration on real user data, so it needs the golden fixture (FR-D1's binding) to pass and a pre-migration backup per charter 11b.3. Cheaper alternative worth considering: leave the columns, delete nothing, but add the filter to the read paths so the column means what it says. That was NOT chosen because it implements a feature nobody asked for; recorded here so the next agent does not have to re-derive the trade-off.

BINDING. tests/storage/retrieval-integrity.test.ts asserts the column exists and is ignored by getAll(). That test is deleted along with the columns.</parameter>
</invoke>

title: FR-D3 T6/T7 — getByFile treats underscore as a LIKE wildcard, and snapshot_cache.ttl_minutes is written but never enforced
description:
Two independent defects, both PROVEN, filed together because both are small and both are in the same domain doc section.

T6 — src/repositories/decisions.repo.ts:116-119. getByFile runs `affected_files LIKE ?` with `%path%`. The value IS bound, so this is NOT an injection — but LIKE metacharacters in the path are not escaped and underscore is a single-character wildcard. MEASURED: getByFile("src/pocx/file_notes.repo.ts") returned BOTH file_notes.repo.ts and file-notes.repo.ts. Underscores are pervasive in this codebase's own filenames, so it over-matches in ordinary use, and the caller cannot tell — decisions about a different file are presented as governing this one. It is also a substring match against a JSON array, so any path is matched by any longer path containing it, e.g. src/a.ts matches src/a.ts.bak.

T6 TARGET. Use `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM json_each(affected_files) WHERE value = ?)` — the exact pattern getFiltered already uses eight lines above it at :108. No escaping needed, no substring semantics, correct by construction. REJECTED: adding ESCAPE '\' and escaping metacharacters — fixes the wildcard but keeps substring matching, so it fixes the symptom found and leaves the class.

T7 — src/repositories/snapshot.repo.ts. upsert() writes ttl_minutes on every call. getCached() selects only value and updated_at, never reads ttl_minutes, and never compares updated_at against now. MEASURED: an entry written with ttl_minutes=5 and updated_at=2020-01-01 was returned unchanged. Cache entries are immortal.

T7 TARGET. getCached compares updated_at + ttl_minutes against now and returns null when expired. REJECTED: dropping the column as dead weight the way task #66 drops deleted_at — rejected because unlike deleted_at this column has a live writer on every upsert, so an unenforced TTL is a correctness bug rather than dead schema.

BINDING for both. tests/storage/retrieval-integrity.test.ts, describe "Bounds and match semantics". Both assertions are PINNED to today's wrong values: getByFile is asserted to return 2 and must become 1; getCached is asserted non-null and must become null.

Related: task #44 covers the third item in that describe block, the unbounded limit.</parameter>
</invoke>

title: FR-D7 T4 — session start costs 59,705 tokens at verbosity full against a documented ~730, and it is growing
description: PROVEN by docs/foundations/measurements/measure-session-cost.mjs, run twice against the same harness three days apart. 2026-08-02: 48,496 tokens. 2026-08-05: 59,705 tokens, 81.8x the figure the tool description promises the agent at the moment it picks the parameter. Repeat sessions are 55,911, so it is not a first-contact cost. nano is worse proportionally: claimed ~10, measured 2,021, 202x. The only honest tier is agent_role sub at 120 against a claimed 300-500. The growth is the finding, not the absolute number: the payload scales with how much the store remembers, so a memory tool gets more expensive to orient in the more it has remembered. project_snapshot alone was 153,194 of the 246,118 characters returned to this session. Fix bounds the response and makes the documented figure a tested assertion rather than prose.

title: FR-D7 T2 — every CRITICAL agent rule gets a mechanism or is deleted; AR-01 measures 21.1 percent
description:
PROVEN by docs/foundations/measurements/measure-rule-compliance.mjs. Of the 114 distinct files this project has edited since it began using Engram on itself, 24 ever received a change row. AR-01 is priority CRITICAL and is replayed into every agent context at every session start. AR-02 is worse: 3 of the 19 sessions with telemetry called get_file_notes at all. AR-03 is the best at 27 of 34. Nothing in src detects, blocks or counts a violation of any of the eight. The closest thing is WorkflowAdvisorService, which is session-scoped, in memory, capped at five nudges, never keyed to a rule id, and disablable by config. The decisive evidence is that the product already concedes the rule does not work: the git post-commit hook handler at src/index.ts lines 38 to 41 says in its own comment that it records commits so the history stays complete even when an agent does not call record_change. The mechanism that does AR-01's job automatically already ships. The target is to delete the rule and promote the mechanism, not to restate the rule more loudly.

── EXAMINED 2026-08-07 AND DELIBERATELY NOT IMPLEMENTED ──

The rules live at src/tools/find.ts:291-300, eight entries in AGENT_RULES. Deleting AR-01 is a two-line edit. I stopped anyway, and the reason is a gap in the target as written, not reluctance.

THE MECHANISM IS NOT INSTALLED BY DEFAULT. The post-commit hook arrives only via `engram install --install-hooks` or engram_admin(action:"install_hooks"). So "delete the rule and promote the mechanism" is sound only where the hook exists. Delete AR-01 today and every user without the hook loses change recording entirely rather than losing 79% of it — a strict regression for them, dressed as a cleanup. The measurement proves the rule does not work; it does not prove the mechanism is present.

FOUR THINGS THE MECHANISM DOES NOT COVER, none of which the 21.1% figure separates out: uncommitted work (the whole of a session until the first commit); work in a repo with no git; the "why", since a commit message is not the rationale record_change carries; and any machine where the hook was never installed. AR-01's replacement has to answer all four or the deletion trades a rule nobody follows for a mechanism nobody has.

SO THE HONEST SEQUENCE IS THREE STEPS, and only the first two are safe to take without a human decision:
  1. MAKE THE MECHANISM VISIBLE. Session start reports whether the post-commit hook is installed. You cannot promote a mechanism you cannot see, and right now neither the agent nor the user can tell. Additive, one boolean, no behaviour change. Cheap — but note session start is already measured at ~48,500 tokens at full verbosity, so it must be one line, not a block.
  2. MEASURE THE MECHANISM THE WAY AR-01 WAS MEASURED. Re-run measure-rule-compliance.mjs split by hook-installed vs not. If change coverage with the hook is not near-total, the mechanism does not replace the rule and this task's premise is wrong. That check has never been run and the whole target rests on it.
  3. THEN delete AR-01 — or keep it, scoped to what the hook cannot see (uncommitted work and rationale), which is a smaller and truthful rule rather than a louder one.

WHY I DID NOT JUST DO STEP 1. Engram is published with wide adoption (charter settled input 1). AR-01 is CRITICAL and reaches every agent in every session on every install; changing what session start emits changes behaviour for every user of 1.13.0 onward. That is a product decision, and the maintainer asked for design-consequence items to be documented for review rather than implemented. Step 1 is the cheapest thing here and still crosses that line.

REJECTED — install the hook by default so the mechanism is always present. It is the obvious way to make deletion safe and it is the wrong trade: writing into .git/hooks unasked is the H1 hazard class this project fixed in e039fdc, where the CLI destroyed a pre-existing husky hook. The write is safe NOW (append, backup, refuse-if-foreign, union-shaped recognition in src/git-hook.ts) but "safe to do when asked" is not "right to do unasked". If it is ever done it belongs behind an explicit prompt in the installer, defaulted to yes, not behind a rule deletion.

BLOCKS NOTHING. Left backlog rather than in_progress: no code changed, and the next agent should start at step 2, which is a measurement, not an edit.

title: FR-D7 T6 — a dispatcher's self-description must be generated from its own action enum, not hand-maintained
description: VERIFIED by deriving both lists from source. engram_admin declares 37 actions and its description names 30, silently omitting install_hooks, remove_hooks, generate_report, get_global_knowledge, get_instance_info, import_from_instance and set_instance_label. engram_memory declares 38 and omits get_knowledge. This is the description an agent reads before deciding whether to call the tool at all, so an omitted action is one that an agent which never calls engram_find may never learn exists. It also undermines catalog tiering, which deliberately sends less on repeat contact on the assumption that first contact was complete. Generate the list from the enum the way CAPABILITY-SURFACE.md is already generated, so it cannot drift again. Pinned as a DEFECT assertion in tests/ergonomics/surface-honesty.test.ts, which asserts today's wrong omission lists and therefore breaks when this is fixed.

title: FR-D7 T1 — one flattened schema advertises 79 optional parameters for actions that accept one
description: VERIFIED by counting the top level of the inputSchema. engram_memory declares 79 optional top-level parameters covering all 38 of its actions, and nothing in the schema indicates which apply to the action being called. engram_admin declares 32 for 37 actions. The measured consequence: record_change advertises file_path, change_type and description at the top level, all three are ignored, and the handler at dispatcher-memory.ts line 415 rejects the call because it requires a changes array. FR-D7 hit this on its first write of the session, minutes after reading a handoff warning about the tool surface, which is the point. The tool's own description concedes the schema is not authoritative by telling the agent to use engram_find to look up exact parameter schemas. This is the structural defect that also produces the advertised owner parameter in task 72, and it is the strongest candidate explanation for the 45 percent ambiguity in the FR-0c distinctness measurement.

title: FR-D7 T7 — update_task advertises an owner parameter, and there is no owner column
description: VERIFIED. The parameter is declared in the engram_memory schema and the handler writes it to claimed_by around dispatcher-memory.ts line 623. That conflates an assigned owner with an atomic claim lock, which are two different concepts behind one advertised name, and it matters because FR-D4 established that a crashed agent's claim is unreclaimable. Setting an owner therefore takes a lock the caller did not know they were taking. Inherited from handoff 8, re-verified here. Either rename the parameter to claimed_by so the surface says what it does, or give tasks a real owner column distinct from the lock. Do not add an owner column merely to make the advertised name true; no feature has asked for one. Pinned as a DEFECT assertion in tests/ergonomics/surface-honesty.test.ts.

title: FR-D7 T3/T5 — the session-start payload re-sends what the agent already has, and embeds a changelog it cannot act on
description: Two halves of one defect in what session start chooses to send. First, VERIFIED: selectCatalogTier at sessions.ts lines 36 to 44 tracks per-agent delivery through a catalog_delivered config key and degrades a returning agent to names only, which is exactly the right design. The identical mechanism is never applied to agent_rules, which are spread unconditionally into every response at sessions.ts lines 296, 494 and 508, with no gating and no rules_delivered key anywhere in src. The project built the solution and used it for the cheaper payload. Second, REPORTED and worth confirming before acting: update_available embeds raw release-notes markdown fetched from npm or the GitHub Releases API, measured at 22.2 percent of a summary response in FR-0c. An agent can do nothing with a changelog. Send an installed version, an available version and a URL. Note the trust dimension for FR-D2: that markdown is third-party text placed directly into an agent's context, and agent-rules.service.ts carries a comment describing a prior removed bug of exactly that shape.

title: FR-D9 T4 — STATE.md gets a real gate, or stops claiming currency it cannot have
description:
STATE.md is the only generated artifact in the repo with NO gate of any kind, and the binding its own generator names does not exist. VERIFIED: generate-state.mjs lines 40 to 44 say the binding is "a local git hook (engram_admin install_hooks) plus this check". The hook that engram_admin install_hooks actually installs (dispatcher-admin.ts lines 358 to 374) only appends commit metadata to .engram/git-changes.log. It never touches the database and never invokes generate-state.mjs. Nothing anywhere invokes it: state and state:check exist only as package.json scripts, referenced by no hook, no workflow and no code.

This closes observation #91 and reverses its conclusion. #91 diagnosed a sequencing problem, and FR-D7's inverted ordering did work — STATE.md arrived current for FR-D9, the first time in four handovers. But that is a workaround for a symptom. The cause is a missing mechanism, and three consecutive agents followed the process correctly and still handed over a misdirecting file because there was nothing to fail.

CI cannot gate this: the source is .engram/memory.db and .gitignore excludes it. That is not a bug — the database is genuinely local. Rejected: committing the database, because it carries machine_id, http_token and instance_id and charter 11b.1 already sanitises a fixture for exactly this reason. Rejected: relying on ordering discipline, because charter 7.5 says that is not a binding.

CHOSEN: a pre-commit hook that regenerates STATE.md when .engram/memory.db is newer than docs/STATE.md, plus an honest header. The hook is local, which is the right scope because the staleness is local. FALLBACK, and it is explicitly the honest option rather than a lesser one: keep state:check manual and DELETE the "never hand-edit / kept true by" claim from both the file and the generator header. An artifact that overstates its own guarantees is the Post Office Horizon failure in miniature — a system of record trusted because it looks authoritative.

Pinned by tests/process/anti-drift.test.ts as a DEFECT: the registry classifies docs/STATE.md as UNGATED against this task, and asserts ci.yml contains neither state:check nor generate-state.mjs. Shipping a gate breaks those assertions and forces them to be edited in the same commit.</content>
</invoke>

title: FR-D9 T1 — the capability surface must render parameter descriptions; it is blind to the exact defect FR-D7 found
description:
PROVEN by experiment on branch fr/d9-process. A deliberately false per-parameter description, compiled into the shipped tool schema, passes node scripts/generate-capability-surface.mjs --check at exit 0. The control — adding one optional parameter to the same schema — fails it at exit 1. So the gate catches structural drift exactly as designed and is completely blind to semantic drift. Both probes were reverted and the tree left clean.

Cause VERIFIED: generate-capability-surface.mjs line 42 captures config.description, the TOOL-level description. describeType() never reads Zod's per-field .description, the property that .describe() sets. So CAPABILITY-SURFACE.md renders types, enums, bounds and required/optional, and no parameter prose at all.

Why this is critical rather than cosmetic. FR-D7 proved AR-01 compliance at 21.1 percent and traced the cause to record_change advertising file_path, change_type and description while ignoring all three and requiring a changes array. That defect IS a description telling an agent something false. The gate built to keep the agent-facing contract honest cannot read the part of the contract that lied, could not have caught it, and would not catch its return.

Rejected: a lint rule requiring every parameter to have a description — it enforces presence, not truth, and FR-D7's defect was a description that was present and wrong, so it would have passed. Rejected: asserting specific description strings in a test — that is a hand-maintained register, restated rather than derived, which charter section 2 rejects because it fails on every legitimate edit and gets switched off within a week.

CHOSEN: render descriptions into the generated artifact, so a changed description becomes a diff in review. Honest about its ceiling — this is an internal-consistency gate, and the Post Office Horizon material in section 3b is the argument that internal consistency is necessary and not sufficient. It cannot make a description TRUE from inside the same source. Task #77 is the other half.

Note the interaction with DEFERRED-CHANGES D14: rendering descriptions changes CAPABILITY-SURFACE.md content but not the advertised MCP schema, so it is not the consumer-visible contract change D14 gates. It can ship independently.

Pinned by tests/process/anti-drift.test.ts as a DEFECT: the suite asserts the generator holds exactly one .description reference. A second one means this task has shipped and the pin must be edited.</content>
</invoke>

title: FR-D9 T3 — the `enforced` column enforces nothing; make it enforce or rename it
description:
VERIFIED across the whole codebase. Every occurrence of the conventions.enforced column is one of three things: a WHERE enforced = 1 retrieval filter (conventions.repo.ts lines 37, 41, 61, 78; dispatcher-memory.ts line 569; intelligence.ts line 91; cross-instance.service.ts line 318), a sort key (sessions.ts line 318), or the toggle that sets it (conventions.repo.ts lines 85 to 88; dispatcher-memory.ts lines 584 to 587). There is NO code path in which enforced = 1 causes a write to be rejected or a check to run. The column selects what is DISPLAYED. sessions.ts line 325 then ships every packaged PM convention to every agent with a hardcoded enforced: true.

The consequence is measured, not hypothetical. The convention pmconv-traceability reads "Every decision requires a rationale. No undocumented choices." It is violated by 9 of 26 decisions: #16, #17, #18, #19, #20, #22, #23, #24, #26. Six are transport corruption (task #77); three never had a rationale at all. Nothing reported either, because nothing checks.

engram_find(action: lint) exists and can check content against conventions, but nothing calls it automatically, so it is a tool an agent must remember to use — and this project has measured what that is worth at 21.1 percent.

Rejected: wire every convention into a blocking check. Conventions are prose, most are not machine-checkable, and pretending otherwise produces the vacuous gates the Goodhart material in section 3b describes — a coverage bonus that produced more than 25 percent of tests with no assertions at all.

CHOSEN: split the concept. Rename the display semantics to active or surfaced, and reserve enforced for conventions that name a mechanism, mirroring FR-D7's rule registry which made "does a mechanism exist" a step that cannot be skipped. A convention that enforces nothing is still worth surfacing; it is not worth calling enforced, because a reviewer who trusts the word stops checking.

Pinned by tests/process/anti-drift.test.ts: every packaged PM convention must be classified in CONVENTION_ENFORCEMENT as UNENFORCED against this task or name a mechanism that resolves in source. Adding a sixth PM convention fails the suite until someone classifies it.</content>
</invoke>

title: FR-D9 T5 — session-end stats: count by event, not by row ownership (supersedes task #63's framing)
description:
Task #63 is CONFIRMED and its stated cause is CORRECTED. The diagnosis — session end counts rows by exact session_id match — is right. The mechanism blamed, the git hook, is wrong.

VERIFIED: tasks.session_id is stamped once at creation (dispatcher-memory.ts line 595) and update_task NEVER touches it. Its UPDATE builder (dispatcher-memory.ts lines 610 to 634) sets status, completed_at, priority, description, claimed_by, blocked_by, assigned_files, tags and updated_at, and nothing else. So "I closed 7 tasks and it reported 0" happens whenever those tasks were CREATED in an earlier session — the overwhelmingly common case, since tasks are the one record type explicitly designed to outlive a session. No git hook is required for the bug to occur.

The queries are at sessions.ts lines 561 to 565: COUNT(*) FROM changes WHERE session_id = ?, the same over decisions, over tasks WHERE session_id = ? AND status = 'done', and over observations.

Rejected: update session_id on close. It merely moves the lie — the row would then misreport where the task was CREATED, and creation attribution is what the field is for.

CHOSEN: count by event rather than by row ownership. Session-end statistics should read from entries stamped in that session (changes or audit_log), or a completed_in_session column should be added. This feeds task #10's vertical traceability rather than competing with it.

Related and larger, from the same enumeration: no task_id, decision_id or change_id column exists anywhere in the schema. Of roughly 14 session-linking columns, exactly ONE is a declared foreign key (observations.session_id, migrations.ts line 742). PRAGMA foreign_keys IS enabled (database.ts line 120) — so the pragma is correct and nearly moot, since there is almost nothing declared for it to enforce. The only decision-to-change association is affected_files, a JSON array of path STRINGS matched by LIKE and json_each (decisions.repo.ts lines 108 to 119). Decision-to-task and change-to-task have no path at all. So get_file_history's advertised "all changes + decisions for a specific file" is a string join, and it is the only traversal that exists.

Supersedes the framing of task #63; #63 should be closed against this one.</content>
</invoke>

title: FR-D8 T1 — route dispatcher SQL through repositories/ (Law 1), ratchet-guarded
description:
ENGRAM_CONSTITUTION.md:58 Law 1 states "repositories/ owns SQL. services/ owns logic and I/O. tools/ owns MCP dispatch." and calls it "The one clean separation in the codebase. Preserve it." The live product path does not obey it. PROVEN 2026-08-05 on a clean tree at 038aea6: dispatcher-memory.ts has 2 getRepos() calls against 69 .prepare() statements, dispatcher-admin.ts 1 against 22, sessions.ts 4 against 8. That is 7 repository calls against 99 raw ones, a 93% bypass. The 13-repo 1,283-line repository layer is consumed only by src/database.ts and six files under src/services/ — never by the MCP tool surface, which is the product.

This task is NOT "refactor all 91 call sites". The failure literature argues against that as a single move: Carbon Health's 107-incident study of decomposition (arXiv:2505.09813) found it traded database incidents for over-fetching and eventual-consistency incidents rather than reducing them, and recommends in-place modularisation before any hard split. DEFERRED D14 separately says the tool contract is already in flux and T1 there must not merge until packages/* and the HTTP API have a generated surface.

What is already done: tests/codebase/maintainability.test.ts freezes a per-file ceiling on .prepare() counts. A fall is always allowed; a rise fails CI with a message naming the constitution. So the bleeding is stopped without the rewrite, and this task can be paid down incrementally at whatever rate is safe.

Suggested order, cheapest first: (1) the conventions and observations queries in dispatcher-memory, which already have repository equivalents; (2) file_locks and pending_work, which have no repo at all and want one; (3) dispatcher-admin's 22, which are mostly stats and health and may legitimately stay raw — decide explicitly rather than by default. Lower the ceiling in tests/codebase/maintainability.test.ts in the same commit as each reduction, so the number a human reviews is the number that was earned.

title: FR-D8 T2 — generate the file census instead of hand-maintaining it
description:
ENGRAM_CONSTITUTION.md's "Appendix — File census" is hand-typed prose stating eleven numbers about the codebase. On 2026-08-05 FR-D8 re-measured all of them and six of the ten sub-rows were wrong, plus the total: it claimed 90 files / 17,560 lines / ~77% reachable against an actual 91 / 18,353 / ~78%. services/ was listed as 13 files when there are 12. tools/ — live had drifted 261 lines. The only row that held exactly was the dead-code row, and only because that set has not changed since it was written.

This is finding F5's exact shape — a status-bearing claim that is quietly no longer true — inside the document that defines the project's architectural laws. Nobody was careless; nothing recomputes it.

The fix is the survival criterion from the charter and project-state-tracking-design.md §3: couple the number to something that breaks. Write scripts/generate-census.mjs on the pattern already proven three times in this repo (generate-capability-surface.mjs, generate-http-surface.mjs, generate-state.mjs): walk src/, classify by directory, resolve the live/dead split from knip.json's ignore list rather than a hardcoded list, emit the table between markers, and support --check for CI.

Do NOT solve this with a test asserting exact line counts. That was considered and rejected while writing tests/codebase/maintainability.test.ts: a total-line assertion fails on every legitimate code change, which is precisely how a gate becomes permanently red and then ignored — the normalisation-of-deviance path that left the knip gate red from the commit that introduced it until this session. A generator plus --check fails only when the committed table and the tree disagree, which is the real condition.

While doing it, also reconcile CONTRIBUTING.md:257 with vitest.config.ts. The former says "There is no enforced coverage gate today"; the latter sets thresholds of 75/65/75/75 on src/repositories/**. Both are defensible in isolation and together they are a contradiction: CI runs `npm test`, never `npm run test:coverage`, so the configured threshold has never once executed. Decide whether the gate is real and run it, or delete the config.

title: FR-D8 T3 — triage knip's 22 unused exports and 28 unused types, then raise them back to error
description:
FR-D8 made the knip gate green on 2026-08-05 by (a) adding the 15 deliberately-retained dead files to knip.json's ignore list, which is what DEFERRED D10 and task #6 require since those files hold the only record of validation the v1.6 consolidation dropped, and (b) demoting the exports/types/enumMembers/classMembers/duplicates rules from error to warn. (a) is honest. (b) is a deliberate narrowing and this task is the debt it created — recorded rather than left implicit, because a gate quietly doing less than its name suggests is the failure this domain exists to catch.

What is now warned rather than enforced: 22 unused exports and 28 unused exported types. They are still printed on every run, so the signal is visible; it just no longer fails the build.

The reason for narrowing rather than fixing now: the rulesync project's knip issue (github.com/dyoshikawa/rulesync/issues/1763) is a near-exact match — a knip report of 70 unused exports and 217 unused types described as "too noisy to act on as-is" and "effectively left unattended", with some entries turning out to be config-gap false positives rather than real dead code. The standard remediation there is triage-then-enforce, not enforce-then-drown. Knip's own docs concede false positives from dynamic imports and string-keyed dispatch (knip.dev/guides/handling-issues), and this codebase dispatches 38 actions through a string switch, so a fraction of the 50 will be legitimate.

Some entries are already known-live findings and must not be deleted blind: errorWithData in src/response.ts has 0 call sites and is tracked as task #55 because it is the ONE helper already returning the correct JSON envelope shape that DEFERRED D7 wants adopted — deleting it would remove the fix. Treat that as the worked example of why this triage is per-item.

Done when: each of the 50 is classified delete / keep-with-ignore-entry / wire-up, and knip.json's rules go back to "error".

title: FR-D8 T4 — packages/* receive no static analysis at all; DEFERRED D14 describes this wrongly
description:
CORRECTION TO A DEFERRED ENTRY. DEFERRED-CHANGES D14 states that knip "flags them as unused entry points rather than as consumers — so the one tool that might notice is the one that has already been configured to look away." The second half is right about the consequence and wrong about the mechanism, and the mechanism matters because it changes the fix.

VERIFIED 2026-08-05: knip.json sets project to ["src/**/*.ts"]. packages/ is not in project and not in entry. It is not flagged, suppressed, or ignored — it is outside the analysis entirely. PROVEN by running the gate: no packages/* path appears anywhere in knip's output, in any severity. .github/workflows/ci.yml:75-76 comments that "knip.json is scoped to src/; packages/* are separate build entry points and would drown the signal", which describes a suppression of noise. There is no noise to suppress because there is no analysis.

Why this is worth a task rather than a footnote. Three packages ship to users — engram-dashboard (29 files), engram-thin-client, engram-universal-thin-client. They are consumers of the HTTP API. Charter §11b.1 and D14 both flag that a response-envelope change in FR-D6, or the per-action schema reshape in FR-D7 T1, can break them with nothing reporting it. generate-http-surface.mjs now gates the API's shape, which is the producer side. Nothing at all looks at the consumer side, so a dashboard file that stops being reachable after an API change is invisible.

Action: give packages/* their own knip workspace configuration, or a second knip config run as a separate CI step so its noise cannot drown the src/ signal (which is the legitimate concern the ci.yml comment was reaching for). Start with warnings only and triage per T3's pattern before enforcing.

Also update DEFERRED D14's "Would it be caught otherwise?" paragraph, which currently rests on the wrong mechanism.

title: FR-D10 T1 — remove the false network-access denial from main's SECURITY.md (documentation only, NOT a release)
description: RELEASED, NOT REDONE — FR-Phase2-Item0, 2026-08-05. It was in_progress and claimed by session 38, which prepared the work but could not finish it: finishing means publishing, and publishing to main is the maintainer's call. Leaving it claimed would have made the next agent either block on an absent owner or silently rebuild work that already exists, so the claim is released and the work is pinned here instead. THE WORK EXISTS AND IS VERIFIED: branch fix/d10-security-policy-corrections at commit 1ffe9bc, cut from main, not merged and not pushed. It corrects three false claims on the published security policy, not the one this title names: (1) the network-access denial — main has three outbound call sites, update.service.ts, installer/index.ts and agent-rules.service.ts, and SECURITY.md named one; (2) the "no HTTP server / no authentication surface" denial — express, cors and ws are runtime dependencies and index.ts:139-141/:156/:243 opt in, ensure a token and listen on 127.0.0.1; (3) a phantom ~/.engram/memory.db path, the real ones being ~/.engram/global.db and ~/.engram/global/. Checked with FR-D10 test 1's assertion: 3 of 3 named on the fix branch, 0 of 3 on unmodified main. TO FINISH: merge 1ffe9bc into main and push. Nothing else. DO NOT rebuild it — verify the branch still exists first with git log -1 fix/d10-security-policy-corrections.

title: FR-D10 T2 — make the vulnerability reporting channel provably live
description: SECURITY.md is now in package.json files[] (done this session) so it ships in the tarball — previously files was ["dist/"] only, so a user installing from npm got no policy at all, while the only copy that existed (GitHub) was the wrong one. REMAINING: (1) make the email channel direct rather than "the maintainer's email, linked on the GitHub profile" — arXiv:2511.22186 finds email is still the dominant real reporting channel, and arXiv:2510.05604 finds a working link closes reports a median 2 days faster; (2) verify the GitHub private advisory URL actually resolves and advisories are enabled — 0 stars/0 forks/0 watchers means nobody has ever tried it; (3) decide whether the published 48h/7d/30d SLA can be met by a single maintainer. Kill switch: if the SLA is missed once, delete the table the same day and replace with best-effort language. A published SLA already broken is worse than none.

title: FR-D10 T3 — generate and gate the npm tarball manifest
description: What is published is currently an unchecked consequence of files:["dist/"]. PROVEN this session: 367 entries, 1.54MB; SECURITY.md/CONTRIBUTING.md/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md/llms.txt were all absent; all 19 compiled src/tools modules ship INCLUDING the 15 that FR-D8 proved dead (4,057 lines). sourcesContent is absent from the 182 .map files, so original TS is NOT embedded — that specific leak does not occur. ACTION: scripts/generate-tarball-manifest.mjs + --check in CI, on the pattern already proven 3x (capability-surface, http-surface, state). REJECTED: asserting an exact file list in a test — that is FR-D8 T5's rejected pattern, it fails on every legitimate build change and goes permanently red, which is exactly how knip stayed red from 307d2f2 for 9 sessions. Prior art: tiptap#7613 (March 2026) shipped packages with no dist/ at all while CI was green.

title: FR-D10 T4 — state on the public surface that this is a single-maintainer project
description: SECURITY.md's "we", its 48h/7d/30d SLA table, and its acknowledgements section all read as an organisation. The document creates that impression and the document should correct it. ACTION: say plainly that governance, CoC enforcement and the security SLA are one person, best-effort. REJECTED: adopting a fuller governance document — Rust's entire moderation team resigned in Nov 2021 stating they were "unable to enforce the Rust Code of Conduct"; the documents existed, the enforcement capacity did not. For a single maintainer, more process text only widens the gap between stated and real, which is this domain's whole failure mode. REJECTED: saying nothing because it is obvious from commit history — it is obvious only to someone who looks, and the docs actively suggest otherwise.

title: Charter §10.4 — define recall to include generated re-exports and write-call responses
description: Both pre-registered suppression arms leaked, through three channels (observation #108). (1) STATE.md is generated FROM Engram memory and is the file every agent is told to read first — third identical occurrence. (2) NEW: record_decision's response returned 4 similar decisions WITH FULL RATIONALES; that is content, not a prompt, arriving on a WRITE. (3) The _advisor field urges get_decisions on write calls. ACTION: amend charter §10.4 to state that generated re-exports of Engram memory and stored content returned by write calls both count as recall; add a header line to STATE.md naming itself as a recall channel, so a future suppressed arm is told at the point of reading. REJECTED: instructing agents not to read STATE.md — STATE.md:83 is literally "Where to go next: 1. This file", and an instruction contradicting the entry-point document will lose. REJECTED: declaring the arms void — the interactive channel was fully suppressed and what leaked is bounded enumerable prose; voiding discards the only control data the experiment has. The leak is a limit (§10.6), not a disqualification, and R3 must be read as "no detectable difference GIVEN a leaked summary".

title: Log recall events at the time they happen, so instrument 1 can be sampled rather than reconstructed
description: Charter §10.2 assumes a sample of recall events exists. It never did — which, more than any verdict, is why the primary instrument went nine domains without running. tool_call_log records THAT a recall action was called (since 5ff7e2f) but not what it returned or what the agent did next. FR-D10's run had to reconstruct n=14 from the domain docs' own citations, which biases toward recalls a document bothered to cite. ACTION: record recall events — action, what was returned, session — so a future run draws a sample instead of rebuilding one. WITHOUT THIS, no future run does better than n=14. ALSO FIX THE DESIGN: FR-D10 used two judges over DISJOINT halves, so there is no inter-rater agreement statistic at all (judge A returned 0 REQUIRED, judge B returned 1). Overlapping assignment costs one more round and should be the default next time. And do not repeat FR-D10's sampling error: enriching the sample for known-wrong records makes the MISLEADING rate uninterpretable (observation #106).

title: engram_session verbosity:"nano" returns ~5,000 chars, not the documented ~10 tokens
description: The tool schema documents verbosity nano as "counts+rules only (~10 tokens)". Called with intent:"quick_op" + verbosity:"nano" this session, the response included agent_rules (8 rules), the full tool_catalog (75 action names) AND update_available carrying the entire 4,966-character v1.12.0 changelog. The verbosity contract does not gate update_available or the catalog at all. This is a public-surface claim in the sense D10 owns: the tool description is what an agent reads to choose a parameter, and it is wrong by two orders of magnitude. It also matters for the token-cost work: Trellis/D3 already flag ~660 tokens/session of AGENT_RULES + tier-0 catalog as a real win, and this is a larger one hiding behind a parameter that claims to suppress it. ACTION: gate update_available and tool_catalog by verbosity, or correct the documented figure. Feeds FR-D7 ergonomics.

title: Public-surface binding is blind to version ranges — SECURITY.md understated the affected release
description: FOUND AND FIXED THIS SESSION, but the gap that allowed it is still open. SECURITY.md on v2-foundations said "Up to and including v1.11.0 this was not true" about the agent-rules fetch. PROVEN false: 87712f4 (the fix) is not an ancestor of main, main's package.json is 1.12.0, and npm latest is 1.12.0 — so v1.12.0, the currently published release, DOES fetch. A user on latest reading that sentence concludes they are unaffected. Corrected to v1.12.0 in this session. WHY THE BINDING MISSED IT: FR-D10 test 1 asserts every fetch site in src/ is NAMED in SECURITY.md. It passed, because the section names the mechanism correctly — it was the VERSION RANGE that was wrong, and no assertion reads version claims. This is the second time a carefully hand-corrected SECURITY.md was still wrong (D10 section 5 records the first, off by one fetch site). ACTION: add an assertion that any "up to and including vX.Y.Z" claim about a removed mechanism resolves against git — specifically that the commit removing the mechanism is not an ancestor of main when the claim names a version at or below main's package.json version. Cheaper alternative worth considering first: assert that SECURITY.md never names a version lower than main's published version when describing a still-live defect.

title: knip is the one gate still CI-only, so it is still exposed to the workflow-divergence defect item 0 was raised over — decide: run it offline-capable inside npm test, or accept CI-only in writing
description:
DESCRIPTION RESTORED 2026-08-06 BY SESSION 43. This row's description column was NULL — not empty, NULL — the convention-#7 transport corruption, on a row the master plan cites by number in section 2.3. The title survived; everything else was lost. Reconstructed from the master plan's own section 2.3 text, which states the residual in full, and from .github/workflows/ci.yml. Marked as reconstruction rather than presented as the original, per convention #2's principle: a repaired record that does not say it was repaired is a second false claim.

THE RESIDUAL. Master plan item 0a moved the two generator gates — generate-capability-surface.mjs --check and generate-http-surface.mjs --check — inside npm test, so they execute on every branch under either workflow, locally before a push rather than only after one, and they travel with a cherry-pick. knip did NOT move. It is still a bare run: step in .github/workflows/ci.yml, verified at the "Check for dead code" step, so it remains exposed to the exact cross-branch workflow-divergence defect that item 0 was raised over: main and v2-foundations carry different workflow files, and tests/process/anti-drift.test.ts can only ever read the workflow on the branch running it, so it is structurally incapable of noticing the divergence.

WHY IT WAS LEFT CI-ONLY. npx -y knip@5 needs the network, and a gate that cannot pass offline is a gate a developer switches off. tests/process/ci-parity.test.ts carries a ratchet that fails the suite if any run: step in ci.yml is neither mirrored into npm test nor classified CI-only against a task — this task is that classification, which is why the row existing matters more than its priority suggests.

THE DECISION, WHICH IS THE WHOLE TASK. Either (a) make knip offline-capable and move it inside npm test like its two siblings, for example by adding it as a devDependency so no network fetch is needed at run time, or (b) accept CI-only in writing, with the acceptance recorded as a decision naming what the project loses — namely that this one gate is not verifiable before a push and not carried by a cherry-pick, so Release A would not have inherited it had item 0b not ported the inputs separately.

STATUS INPUT, PROVEN 2026-08-06: npx -y knip@5 --no-progress now exits 0 on v2-foundations, so the gate is green and the question is purely about where it runs, not whether it passes. Adjacent rows: #79 asks for the green that has already landed and should be closed; #82 owns the demoted rules and the ignore list that produced the green.

title: 2.0.0 must edit the N3 DEFECT pin on release/1.13.0 — mcp-wire.test.ts asserts that `end` ignores session_id and closes the newest open session, which f234052 fixes
description:
DESCRIPTION RESTORED 2026-08-06 BY SESSION 43. This row's description column was NULL — not empty, NULL — the convention-#7 transport corruption, on a row that gates Release B. The title survived and happens to name both the file and the mechanism, which is luck, not design. Reconstructed from the master plan's section 4.3 release note, which records the same finding in full. Marked as reconstruction rather than presented as the original.

WHAT HAPPENED, from master plan section 4.3. While assembling release/1.13.0 one inherited test broke, and it was invisible until run. tests/e2e/mcp-wire.test.ts's error-envelope pin probed engram_session end with session_id 999999 and depended on a rejection that ONLY commit f234052 introduces — and f234052 is the excluded breaking commit, deliberately held back for 2.0.0 because it makes agent_name required. On the release tree the probe returned SUCCESS rather than the expected error. The probe was changed to use acknowledge_handoff, which errors on both trees, so the suite is honest on the release line.

THE UNDERLYING TRUTH, NOW PINNED AS A DEFECT. engram_session action end IGNORES session_id entirely and closes the newest open session. That behaviour is asserted, on purpose, on release/1.13.0. f234052 fixes it.

WHAT 2.0.0 MUST DO. When f234052 lands on the release line for 2.0.0, the pinned assertion in tests/e2e/mcp-wire.test.ts MUST be edited in the same commit that lands the fix, so it asserts the corrected behaviour rather than the defect. If the fix lands and the pin does not move, the suite goes red and the likely reaction is to weaken the test, which is master plan kill switch 3 exactly: a domain target implemented with its binding edited to make it pass is the pinned-defect permission slip D4 and D9 both warn about. The difference here is that editing this pin IS correct, and the commit must say so.

THE TRANSFERABLE LESSON, recorded in the plan and worth keeping on this row: a test suite cherry-picked out of its own history does not necessarily test what its name says. This defect was invisible to reading and only appeared on execution.

RELATED: task #62 and FR-D4 T4 cover agent_name being self-asserted and unvalidated, which is the same session-identity surface. Task #49 holds the release/1.13.0 assembly detail. Do not attempt this before Release A publishes.

title: Re-tamper every process binding with the VERBATIM original defect text, recovered from git — not with a composed example
description:
FROM OBSERVATION #125, PROVEN 2026-08-06. The docs-router binding was tampered four ways, went red on all four, and was believed — then failed to catch the actual sentence it was written for. "All 90 `src/` files" is digit, space, backticked path, space, noun, and the assertion required the noun to follow the digit directly. All four earlier tampers had been composed from my own regex, so they tested that the gate catches what the author had in mind. That is confirmation, not verification, and it is charter §3b's "researching to confirm" in binding form.

WHAT TO DO. For each assertion in tests/process/*.test.ts, recover the text the assertion was written against — `git show <commit>:<path>` for the state BEFORE the fix — paste it back verbatim, and confirm red. Not a paraphrase. Not an example. The bytes.

ALREADY DONE, SO DO NOT REDO: (1) docs-router.test.ts — found blind, widened to allow up to two word-shaped intervening tokens, re-proven against the verbatim sentence and against "11 currently open tasks", real file green. (2) claude-md.test.ts assertion 3 — a real CRLF prism zone block was appended as prism would emit it and the suite went red; the JS `$` under /m treats a bare \r as a line terminator, so the anchored regex is CRLF-safe. VERIFIED clean, no change needed.

REMAINING: anti-drift.test.ts (4 describe blocks, including the two DEFECT pins) and ci-parity.test.ts (9 tests). Both were read this session and look structurally sound — BANNER splits on /\r?\n/ and trims, which is the correct shape — but "looks sound on a read" is exactly the grade that failed here. Read is not tampered.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS. Master plan §1 is "a capability that is advertised, is described accurately somewhere, and does not execute", found independently in all ten domains. A green binding blind to its own subject is that shape inside the machinery built to prevent it. This one was caught before it shipped, which is the first time in the project that has happened; the others have not been checked.

title: MASTER PLAN item 3 — the 2026-09-16 advisory decision: publish, or record the extension as a decision
description:
CREATED 2026-08-06 BY SESSION 43 BECAUSE THE PLAN'S ONLY DATED COMMITMENT HAD NO ROW. Master plan section 7 item 3 assigned this to task #87. Task #87 is DONE — it was closed as "DEFERRED D11 is stale in its first half — the version regression is already resolved", which is a different piece of work entirely. PROVEN at creation: no open task's title or description contained "advisory", "disclos" or "2026-09-16", and the scheduled_events table held ZERO rows, so the product's own deferred-action mechanism was never used for the one deadline this project has. Handoff #16 called the clock "the one dated commitment on the board" while pointing at the same closed row.

THE COMMITMENT, from master plan section 4.4. A 45-day clock from 2026-08-02, the date the P0 findings were recorded, expiring 2026-09-16. On that date EITHER the security advisory is published OR the reason for extending is written down as an Engram decision. CERT/CC publishes at 45 days regardless of patch status, while warning that gratuitously announcing vulnerabilities may not be in the best interest of public safety — so the clock's purpose is NOT to force disclosure. It is to make continued silence a decision rather than a default.

THIS IS SECTION 9 WORK AND IS THE MAINTAINER'S ALONE. Section 9 item 1 states it plainly: whether to publish an advisory, and when, is a judgement about users, not about code. No agent should publish anything against this row. What an agent MAY do is prepare the draft, verify the reporting channel is live (task #85), and put the decision in front of the maintainer before the date.

WHAT THE ADVISORY WOULD COVER, from section 4.1: four hazards live on published v1.12.0. H1, installer replaces another product's user-level config with a stub on a JSON parse error, no attacker needed. H2, restore reports success and restores nothing. H3, agent rules fetched from a GitHub README and cached to disk, read back with a cast — needs a crafted repo. H4, /export claims "all data" and ships 5 of 24 tables.

INTERLOCK WITH RELEASE A. Master plan kill switch 2 states that if Release A slips past the 45-day clock without a written decision, the hold has become drift and D11's guard has failed — publish the advisory. Release A is assembled and verified on release/1.13.0 at c4fac06 and needs only npm publish plus a push, both the maintainer's, per task #49. The ordinary good outcome is that Release A ships before 2026-09-16 and the advisory accompanies it. Section 4.3 already rejected patching silently with no advisory: Fortinet silently patched a zero-day under active exploitation and left only defenders uninformed, and a patch whose notes omit why is a second false statement one week after removing the first.

ALSO SCHEDULE THE EVENT, do not rely on this row alone. engram_session start surfaces open tasks but nothing surfaces a date; schedule_event with trigger_type datetime and trigger_value 2026-09-16 is the mechanism the product ships for exactly this and it currently holds zero rows.

title: FR-D5 — scripts/install-mcp.js is a second live installer carrying the macOS APPDATA bug that ide-configs.ts documents as fixed
description:
VERIFIED 2026-08-07 by reading both files. scripts/install-mcp.js is a standalone 175-line installer, structurally independent of src/installer/, still wired in package.json:31-32 as `npm run install-mcp` and `npm run install-mcp:list`.

THE DEFECT. Its line 20 reads `const APPDATA = process.env.APPDATA || path.join(HOME, ".config")`. src/installer/ide-configs.ts:20 quotes that exact expression in a comment as the code it replaced, stating it produced the WRONG value on macOS, and the corrected form at ide-configs.ts:25-26 branches on IS_WINDOWS first. So a defect this project identified, documented and fixed is still executing in a parallel copy that ships in the repository and is invocable by name.

BLAST RADIUS, STATED HONESTLY. package.json files is dist/ only (task #86 measured 367 entries), so this file does NOT reach npm users. It reaches anyone who clones the repository and follows a README or a habit to `npm run install-mcp` — contributors, and the maintainer. That makes it lower severity than a shipped defect and higher than dead code, because it is a live npm script whose name is the obvious one to reach for.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE ONE LINE. This is the sixth or seventh instance of the project's recurring pattern in a new position: not a capability that cannot be reached, but a SECOND implementation of a capability that can. knip does not flag it because knip.json's project glob is src/**/*.ts, so scripts/ is outside the analysis entirely — the same blind spot task #83 records for packages/.

DO, and the choice is the task: either DELETE the file and its two package.json scripts, or make the scripts delegate to src/installer. Deleting is preferred and is what the cut list's rule requires — every advertised capability must execute and something must fail when it stops; a second installer satisfies neither half.

REJECTED: fix the APPDATA line and keep the file — that preserves two installers with one bug fixed, which is the state that produced this finding. The next divergence is then invisible again. REJECTED: leave it and document it as legacy — section 3.2 of the master plan rejects documenting a limitation instead of deleting, by name.

BEFORE DELETING: check whether README.md, docs/installation.md or any release note instructs a user to run `npm run install-mcp`. If any does, that text is part of this task. Full audit in observation #127.

title: FR-D5 — CI runs Linux only, so every Windows and macOS installer path branch is dead in CI, and runInstaller has no test caller at all
description:
TWO GAPS WITH ONE CONSEQUENCE, both VERIFIED 2026-08-07. Engram's primary job on first contact is writing platform-specific config paths into other products' files, and neither the platform branches nor the orchestrator that drives them is exercised.

GAP 1, PROVEN. .github/workflows/ci.yml:17 is `runs-on: ubuntu-latest`; the matrix at :21 varies node-version only. src/installer/ide-configs.ts computes IS_WINDOWS and IS_MAC once at import from process.platform, so both are ALWAYS false in CI. Every Windows APPDATA path, every macOS Library/Application Support path, and the requiresCmdWrapper npx wrapper that only Claude Code and Claude Desktop set, are therefore never executed by any CI run. The existing test for the cmd wrapper builds a synthetic IdeDefinition by hand rather than using IDE_CONFIGS, which is an implicit admission that the real object cannot be tested this way on Linux. Note the history: ide-configs.ts:20-24 records that this exact area already shipped a wrong macOS value once.

GAP 2, VERIFIED by search. runInstaller (src/installer/index.ts:172) has zero test callers, and so do all three ide-detector.ts exports — detectCurrentIde, resolveIdeGlobalPaths, detectInstalledIdes. detectInstalledIdes carries a commented FLAW-9 regression fix for false-positive IDE detection with no test protecting it. Everything proven about config-writer.ts is proven in isolation; nothing proves the chain from argv to a written file.

WHY THESE ARE ONE TASK. Adding an OS matrix without an end-to-end test multiplies runs of a suite that does not touch the orchestrator. Adding the end-to-end test without an OS matrix runs it on the one platform whose branches are already covered. Either alone buys little; together they close the class.

DO: (1) add an os matrix to the test job — ubuntu, windows, macos — accepting the CI-minutes cost, and make the platform-dependent tests assert against IDE_CONFIGS rather than a hand-built stand-in. (2) Add the smoke test that drives runInstaller against a temp HOME and asserts the file on disk is what addToConfig alone would have produced. That is the test that proves wiring rather than parts.

REJECTED: stub process.platform in the existing Linux-only suite. It would exercise the path-building branches, which is genuinely useful, but it cannot catch anything about how a real filesystem behaves — case-insensitivity, path length limits, permissions — and it would let the matrix question be declared answered when it is not. Worth doing IN ADDITION, not INSTEAD.

REJECTED: leave it and rely on manual testing before release. That is the status quo, and task #48 already established that the last publish was an unreproducible manual workstation build.

CONSTRAINT: runInstaller calls process.exit() on most branches, so the smoke test needs either an injectable exit or a child-process invocation. Prefer the child process — it tests the real entry point, which is the point of the test. Full audit in observation #127.

title: A parameter the selected action ignores must be an error, not a wider result
description:
From observation #130, where the mechanism and the evidence are. VERIFIED 2026-08-07 at src/tools/dispatcher-memory.ts.

TWO CONCRETE INSTANCES, both silent, both widening: get_tasks accepts `query` (shared schema line 261) and its handler never reads it — the SQL is built from status, priority, tag and limit only. get_file_notes accepts `file_path_filter` and never reads it — that parameter is wired to get_decisions alone (line 552). The second returned all 96 notes at 99,655 characters and overflowed the tool result; the call had been made specifically to keep the read small.

DO, in this order. FIRST implement the two, because they are small and they stop the bleeding today: get_tasks gains a keyword filter (fts_tasks is populated, so MATCH is available and cheap), get_file_notes honours file_path_filter as a LIKE. THEN the structural fix, which is the point of the task: engram_memory takes ONE flat Zod schema for ~40 actions, so every parameter validates for every action and the schema can never say "not for this one". Derive a per-action consumed-parameter map from the handlers and reject anything the selected action does not consume.

DERIVE IT, do not restate it. A hand-kept map of action -> parameters is the same defect one layer up, and this project has now hit that shape four times (installer filename rule FR-D5, addToConfig #127, the cross-instance whitelist F4, the FTS trigger set #35). The write-integrity binding is the worked example: tests/security/write-integrity-coverage.test.ts derives its list from the registration site rather than a glob or a literal.

NOTE the capability-surface gate does NOT catch this and cannot. It derives from the Zod schemas, which are accurate; the divergence is between schema and handler, and nothing reads both. That is arguably the more valuable follow-up — a gate that compares declared parameters against consumed ones would have caught both of these on the commit that introduced them.

WHY IT IS HIGH AND NOT MEDIUM: CLAUDE.md instructs every agent to filter reads rather than pull the board whole, and on these paths that instruction cannot be complied with and the agent cannot tell. The failure is always in the direction of more context, on exactly the calls made to save it.

title: IdeDefinition.envVar is declared, implemented, and assigned by no IDE
description:
Last open item from observation #127, and the only one I did not act on. VERIFIED 2026-08-07: `envVar?: string` is declared at src/installer/ide-configs.ts:55 and NO IDE definition assigns it. The only other mentions in that file are two comments (lines 120, 137) explaining why Windsurf and Gemini CLI deliberately do not use it. The consuming branch at src/installer/config-writer.ts:90 — `if (ide.envVar && !ide.workspaceVar) entry.env = { ENGRAM_PROJECT_ROOT: ide.envVar }` — is therefore unreachable for every IDE the installer supports.

NOT DELETED ON PURPOSE. Removing a typed extension point is a design call rather than a defect fix, and the two comments carry real knowledge that would be orphaned by the deletion: they record that Windsurf expands ${env:VAR_NAME} and Gemini CLI expands only real OS env vars, which is WHY neither can use an IDE-side workspace placeholder in an env value. That reasoning is the expensive part; the field is the cheap part.

DECIDE ONE OF: (a) delete envVar and the branch, moving those two comments to wherever the env-injection decision is now recorded, so the knowledge outlives the field; (b) keep it and assign it for the IDEs that genuinely do expand workspace variables in env values, which is what it was built for and would make the branch live; (c) keep it as an explicit extension point with a comment saying so, and add it to knip.json's ignore with a pointer here so the dead-surface gate stops being silent about it.

Prefer (a) or (b) over (c). This is the seventh instance of the project's implemented-but-unreachable pattern (see D3-C11 on deleted_at, which is the purest — schema and nothing else), and (c) is how the previous six survived.

Note knip does NOT flag this: envVar is a used field on a used interface, so static dead-code analysis sees a live reference. It was found by reading, and only because #127's sub-agent went looking.

title: Publishing a fix does not reach machines already running the vulnerable build — nothing owns the distribution gap
description:
PROVEN 2026-08-10 by `engram install --check` on the maintainer's machine, three days after v1.13.0 was published as `latest`: SEVEN config entries across four products still launch v1.12.0 — Visual Studio (~/.mcp.json), Gemini CLI (~/.gemini/settings.json), JetBrains (~/.config/github-copilot/intellij/mcp.json), and all four Android Studio config directories (2025.3.2, 2025.3.4, 2026.1.2, 2026.1.3). Three further entries are stamped `v?`, the pre-tracking era, so older still. Every one of them has all four P0 findings live.

D11 in docs/DEFERRED-CHANGES.md said "published v1.12.0 is the vulnerable build — every installation on 1.12.0 currently has all four P0s live." Publishing fixed the first half. It never spoke about INSTALLED copies and that half survived the release.

TWO MECHANISMS, BOTH ALREADY RECORDED, NEVER JOINED UP. (1) npx caches per exact spec string and never re-checks the registry, so the README's bare `npx -y engram-mcp-server` served an April build indefinitely — fixed in d354172 by pinning @latest. (2) The installer's fix for the same defect writes a PINNED EXACT VERSION into the IDE config, which is correct and means Engram NO LONGER SELF-UPGRADES. A machine that installed 1.12.0 stays on 1.12.0 until a human re-runs the installer.

So the successor question to D11 is not "should we publish" — that is answered — but "how does a published fix reach a machine that already has the vulnerable build". Nothing in this repo or ENGRAM-MASTER-PLAN.md owns it.

WHY THIS RAISES THE PRIORITY OF THE ADVISORY. The tripwire's 45-day clock (2026-09-16) was reasoned when publishing was the open decision. An advisory is now the ONLY mechanism that reaches those seven entries, because the upgrade path that would have reached them was deliberately removed to fix a worse bug. That is a trade worth stating explicitly rather than discovering later.

FIRST STEPS, none of which is a code change: (1) decide whether the release notes and README should tell existing users to re-run the installer, since nothing else will; (2) decide whether `--check` reporting an outdated version should be louder than a yellow arrow now that it is the only signal a user gets; (3) decide the advisory question against this evidence rather than against the pre-release framing.

NOT A REGRESSION IN THE PINNING FIX. Pinning was right — an unpinned spec meant _engram_version could claim 1.13.0 beside args launching 1.12.0. This task is the cost that fix made visible, not an argument to revert it.

title: Four widely-used MCP clients are unsupported, and two of them cannot be expressed by IdeDefinition at all
description: REPORTED by the 2026-08-11 delegated audit; paths not re-verified by me. OpenAI Codex CLI — ~/.codex/config.toml global, .codex/config.toml project, TOML with a [mcp_servers.NAME] table. Amazon Q Developer CLI — ~/.aws/amazonq/mcp.json global, .amazonq/mcp.json workspace. Zed — %APPDATA%/Zed/settings.json and ~/.config/zed/settings.json, and its key is `context_servers`, NOT mcpServers or servers. Continue.dev — ~/.continue/config.yaml or .continue/mcpServers/*.yaml, YAML. THE POINT IS NOT THE LIST, IT IS WHAT THE LIST EXPOSES: IdeDefinition types configKey as `"mcpServers" | "servers"` and every read/write path assumes JSON. Codex and Continue are TOML and YAML respectively, and Zed needs a third key. Adding any of them is a schema change plus a serialiser per format, not a new registry row — and a JSON writer pointed at a TOML file would destroy it, which is the config-clobber failure class FR-D5 T2 exists to prevent. Decide the scope question first: does Engram support MCP clients generally, or JSON-config IDEs? The current registry answers the second and the README implies the first. Zed and Amazon Q are the cheap ones (JSON); Codex and Continue are the expensive ones and should not be started without a serialiser abstraction and a round-trip test that proves an unrelated key survives a write.
